newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, US seek to avoid antitrust battles.
newsitem.headline: EU, US seek to avoid antitrust battles.

text.p: The European Commission proposed rules on Friday obliging the U.S. and the European Union to abstain from applying their antitrust laws on the other's territory.

The proposal does not cover investigations into mergers and acquisitions which in the EU are subject to strict deadlines and, therefore, could not be be put on hold while waiting for a decision on the other side of the Atlantic.

Boeing Co has argued that the U.S. should have the lead role in vetting its proposed merger with McDonnell Douglas under a 1991 EU-U.S. cooperation agreement on competition issues which already contains so-called positive comity -- courtesy -- provisions.
But a Commission spokesman reiterated strongly on Friday that the provisions did not apply to mergers.

The Commission's new draft agreement between the EU and the U.S. on the application of positive comity principles in the enforcement of competition laws also specifically excluded mergers. The Commission negotiated the agreement with the U.S, authorities which have given their provisional approval.

"Mergers are not within the scope of the proposed agreement due to EU and US merger legislation, which would not allow a deferral or suspension of action as envisaged by the agreement," the Commission said in a statement.

Boeing filed the $14 billion merger for EU regulatory approval in February, therefore recognising the Commission's jurisdiction. The debate over who should have the lead was recently defused as the Federal Trade Commission, which is also investigating the merger, appears increasingly likely to rule on the deal before the Union.
The Boeing case apart, the Commission says it has many reasons to complain about American attempts to impose its law in Europe.

"The United States has expanded its extra-territorial jurisdiction more than any other country, thereby creating frictions in its bilateral relations with the European Community," Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said in a communication on the proposed draft agreement.

The draft accord aims to strengthen the use of positive comity principles which provide that "where a Party believes that anti-competitive activities, occurring in the territory of the other Party, are adversely affecting its interests, it may request the other Party's competition authority to initiate appropriate enforcement activities".
The requesting party will normally suspend its own investigation if it has begun one.

The FTC in January used the principles to ask the Commission to probe a complaint by airline computer reservation system Sabre Group Holdings Inc, which is controlled by AMR Corp, that it was prevented from competing with a rival European system called Amadeus.
EU governments are expected to give their political consent to the new agreement in September or October after the European Parliament has been consulted.
